$comment: VENQORE LAYOUT LAW v2.0 — the machine-readable source.
VENQORE_LAYOUT_LAW.md says it is 'generated from layout-law.json'. That file did
not exist in the repo, which is why three geometry numbers had already drifted
between the prose and the V6 token files (gutter 20 vs 24, topbar 68 vs 64, rail
248 vs 264). This is that file. It is the single source for card geometry, and
both the JS engine (resources/js/Dashboard/layoutLaw.js) and the PHP sanitizer
(app/Reckoner/LayoutLaw.php) read it rather than restating it.
Nothing here is a preference. Where a number looks arbitrary the derivation is
next to it, and a number with no derivation does not belong in this file.
size(n) = n*unit + (n-1)*gutter.
The gutter is part of the PITCH, not something added between cards. CSS Grid
computes this natively from `gap`. That distinction is the documented
alignment bug: with margin-bottom a 2-row card is 64+64=128px while two
stacked 1-row cards are 64+24+64=152px. As part of the pitch, the 2-row card
spans across the gutter and absorbs it — 2*64 + 1*24 = 152 — and the two line
up exactly. Never implement this by hand; `gap` already does it.

shell.$comment: Three regions and only three. Nothing else may position against the viewport.
shell.$headerComment: header_h == unit. One number, two jobs.
shell.$pushComment: Below this the nav overlays rather than pushes. Found by sweeping every integer width from 320 to 3440, not by picking breakpoints.

$comment: Six categories. Each declares a MAX and an ordered list of FITS.
A fit is cols x rows plus a pixel width floor — the narrowest the card may
render and still use that fit. There is no separate 'minimum size': the
leanest fit IS the minimum.
A card WIDENS BEFORE IT DEGRADES. It only drops to a leaner fit when
widening is exhausted, and degrading trades a column for a row and re-lays
its inside.
Supersedes VENQORE_CARD_BUILDER_BUILD_SPEC.md §7.2 (small/medium/large/full)
and the twelve 2x4..8x8 presets that shipped in DashboardBuilderSheet.jsx.

C2.name: Strip
C2.role: One KPI on one line — label left, value right

C3.name: Metric
C3.role: KPI with delta, sparkline or comparison

C4.name: Panel
C4.role: Ranked list, breakdown, small chart, table excerpt

C6.name: Canvas
C6.role: Hero chart, P&L, cohort grid, map

$comment: A chart may only render a shape it is legal for. Shapes come from the
Reckoner; the first entry in each list is the default.
Candlestick is excluded from the entire system — VenQore has no OHLC data.
Which categories a chart can legibly occupy, leanest first. The first entry
is the legibility floor: rendering the chart below it is a fail, which is
what stopped a pie being persisted at 2x4 under the old preset system.
The floors are a function of how much the mark has to say. A stat is one
number and survives a tile; a heatmap is a two-dimensional grid and needs a
board before its cells are distinguishable.
The last five are legal for no shape, so the editor never offers them. They
are listed anyway because a card persisted before the law may hold one, and a
chart with no entry would fall back to a default that could be below its real
legibility floor.

rankLaw.$comment: Action budget. A card exposes at most its rank-1 actions at rest, and Configure never sits on the card face.

$comment: Currency drops first, then decimals, then magnitude. Full precision belongs
in the ledger, never on a dashboard card, and the exact value is always one
hover away.
A value must never overflow, clip or ellipsize its card. It steps down.

accent.$comment: Mechanism M1. Exactly one accent-filled card per board, and it must be the headline metric. Zero is a fail; two is a fail.

$comment: VENQORE LAYOUT LAW v2.0 §10 — the terminal.
A dashboard has unlimited height, so v1.0 only ever had to defend the horizontal
axis. A terminal is exactly one viewport tall and never scrolls the page, so here
HEIGHT is the scarcer resource — and the worst case is not a phone, it is a
1280x720 laptop, where a maximised browser leaves about 570 usable pixels.
The per-viewport tables in VENQORE_LAYOUT_LAW.md are OUTPUTS of the rules below,
not the rules. Implement the waterfall; the tables are the acceptance criteria.
Every floor here is computed from the type scale and real advance widths. For
example cart_line_full = name 132 + qty stepper 96 + rate 75 + total 130 +
delete 36 + gaps 48 + padding 40 = 559. There is no judgement in it.

floors.$cartMinComment: A cart showing fewer than three lines is not a cart, it is a receipt preview. This is the one place in the law where the vertical axis overrules the horizontal.

$comment: A card that cannot get wider gets TALLER and relays its inside. A pane cannot —
a terminal has no vertical slack — so a pane DEMOTES instead.
Ordered from most to least present. `route` exists because some panes are not a
simultaneous view, they are a STEP: a restaurant server on a phone picks a table,
then takes the order. Squeezing both onto 360x560 is the wrong answer to the
right question.
residency.$rank1Comment: A rank-1 pane may be resident or stacked freely, and sheet or route ONLY where the variant declares an ordered sequence with a guaranteed return path. Never tab: a tab implies peers you switch between at will, and a rank-1 pane needs a guaranteed moment, not a competed-for one.

cart.$capComment: Its floor with the item column grown from a 12-char truncation to a full 40-char product name. Past that, extra width is pure margin — a cart shows the same five columns however wide it is.

fits.label: Name on line 1, controls on line 2
Name and total; tap a line to adjust

tender.$capComment: Its floor plus a 4x40 numeric keypad.

fits.label: Abbreviated total in a sticky bar

catalog.$holdComment: Presence is the information. A catalog you can see beats a richer catalog you have to open a sheet for. It also genuinely shows MORE when given more, so it absorbs surplus width rather than capping.

floor.$comment: The floor plan. Rank 1 on the Table variant: the unit of work is the table, not the sale.

scan.name: Scan
scan.tagline: No catalog. Scanner and keyboard only.
scan.for: Large inventory (>2,000 SKUs), barcode-driven. Pharmacy, hardware, grocery, distribution.
scan.why: A catalog nobody browses is 40% of the screen spent on nothing. Removing it is the single biggest calm-down available.

column.name: Column
column.for: Mixed inventory (200-2,000 SKUs) where staff both scan and browse. General retail.
column.why: The familiar shape, but ranked: the catalog is a column, not a competitor.
column.$degradesComment: On a phone the catalog column becomes a picker sheet — open, choose, close. That is a step, not a hidden pane, and it is exactly the Counter variant. Counter is a first-class choice rather than Column’s failure mode.

row.name: Row
row.tagline: Catalog as a top row of tiles.
row.for: Small inventory (<200 SKUs), fast repeat items. Cafe, bakery, kiosk, pharmacy counter.
row.why: On a wide screen a 2-row tile strip is reachable by thumb and leaves the full width for the cart underneath.
row.$bandComment: The catalog band is asymmetric. The FIRST row of tiles is worth squeezing the cart to its floor of 3 lines for — without it there is no touch picker at all. The SECOND is a convenience, so it may only take height the cart does not need to reach a comfortable 5 lines. That is why a short 1280x720 laptop gets one row and a tall iPad gets two.

grid.name: Grid
grid.tagline: Catalog dominant, cart as a rail.
grid.for: Visual products, walk-up counters, staff who point rather than type. Cafe, QSR, boutique.
grid.why: When the product IS the interface, the cart only needs to confirm.
grid.$sequenceComment: Grid demotes the rank-1 tender to a sheet at every width — when the product IS the interface, the cart only needs to confirm. That is legal only because this sequence exists: pick, review, pay, with a guaranteed way back.

counter.name: Counter
counter.for: Phone and small tablet, market stalls, delivery riders, single-hand use.
counter.why: Below 600px nothing else survives; making it a first-class variant means it is designed, not degraded.

table.name: Table
table.for: Restaurants, cafes with table service, salons, any seat/slot business.
table.why: The unit of work is the table, not the sale. A sale is a property of a table.
table.$sequenceComment: The declared sequence is what lets the rank-1 floor pane become a `route` on a phone: an ordered set of steps with a guaranteed return path.

$comment: Columns or bands is an ASPECT question, not a width question.
Splitting a terminal into columns costs nothing vertically and stacking costs a lot.
So a 768x950 portrait iPad wants BANDS — there is height to spend and no width to
spare — and a 1024x695 landscape iPad wants COLUMNS, exactly the reverse.
Computed once per composition, not scored per width, so the only shape change a
user ever sees on a terminal is the portrait/landscape one.
aspect.$ratioComment: width / height. Above this, columns. At or below, bands.

$comment: VENQORE LAYOUT LAW v2.0 §11 — the document.
Eight of the thirteen document screens are the same file copy-pasted — same
imports, same patchInvoice, same drag-reorder, same scan modal, same profit peek
— with the labels swapped and a handful of fields silently dropped from the
payload. That is WHY `Terms` is decorative on every one of them, why a quotation
has no `Valid until`, and why a debit note never restores stock: a fix applied to
the sales invoice never reached the other seven.
A TYPE IS NOT A SCREEN. It is a configuration — a set of capability switches and
label overrides on one editor. That is what this table is.
Density is a preference — an accountant wants ten line columns, a cashier wants
five — but it is a preference the width has to be able to honour. Below the floor
the law CAPS the density rather than letting the user pick something that will
silently mangle the screen.

nav.$comment: 1708 is where a document surface finally lets the nav expand — the first width at which a 264px sidebar still leaves room for the 10-column table AND the summary panel. Below 1024 the nav is hidden entirely; a document needs its width more than it needs a visible rail.

summaryFallback.$comment: When the summary cannot be a resident column it becomes a STICKY ACTION BAR, not the same panel pinned to the bottom — a 438px bar on a 570px laptop leaves nothing for the document it is summarising. Collapsed it is the total, the balance and the primary action; the breakdown is one tap.

capabilities.$comment: Every distinct capability found across all thirteen screens. This is the definition of what the unified editor must support, and the answer to 'will we lose something': if a cell is filled today it is filled here.

$comment: The category a chart gets when a card is first created.
This was derived by taking index 1 of chartCategories, which is arithmetic, not a
decision — and it put a stat in a C2 Strip, a 4x1 band 64px tall with no room for
a delta pill under the value. The reference board's KPI row is four C3 Metric
cards at the standard 3x2 fit, which is 152px, and that is what a number with a
delta and a sparkline actually needs.
chartCategories still governs what is LEGAL. This governs what you get by default.
